source_refs.note: Topic 7.4.4, printed pages 157-158, as printed, with Quick Check 7.7.

blocks.text: The rate constant is specific for a particular reaction at a certain temperature. Since concentrations are in mol dm⁻³ and the reaction rate is in units of mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. The units for k depend on the order of the reaction and the units of time.

blocks.text_alt: Rate = k[Reactants]ⁿ   where n = order of reaction

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: ‘Rectants’ is a misprint for Reactants: k = Rate / [Reactants]ⁿ.
This equation can be used to determine units of any order of reaction.

blocks.text_alt: k = (mol dm⁻³)¹⁻⁰ s⁻¹;  k = mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

blocks.text: For a first order reaction (n = 1), the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of one reactant.

blocks.text_alt: k = (mol dm⁻³)¹⁻¹ s⁻¹;  k = (mol dm⁻³)⁰ s⁻¹;  k = s⁻¹

blocks.text: Therefore, the units of k for a first order rate constant are s⁻¹.

blocks.text_alt: k = (mol dm⁻³)¹⁻² s⁻¹;  k = mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹;  k = dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

blocks.text: The units of k for a second order rate constant are dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

blocks.text_alt: k = (mol dm⁻³)¹⁻³ s⁻¹;  k = mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹;  k = dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹

blocks.text: Therefore, the units of k for a third order rate constant are dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.

blocks.title: Quick Check 7.7
blocks.text:
a) Calculate the overall order of reactions which have the rate expressions:
i) rate = k[NO]² [NH₃]⁰
ii) rate = k[BrO₃][Br⁻][H⁺]²
b) Why do you think chemists want to know the order of a reaction and the rate constant for a reaction?
c) Why the sum of the coefficients of a balanced chemical equation is not necessarily important to give the order of a reaction?

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The bromate ion is BrO₃⁻: rate = k[BrO₃⁻][Br⁻][H⁺]².
